title: The shape of an argument
grammar: Nominalisation and word formation for academic style

scene.speaker: nova
scene.bubble: Turn opinions into arguments — and verbs into nouns. Learn nominalisation and the confident, impersonal language of academic style.
scene.intro: An opinion is easy to state; an argument has to be built. In this unit our reading club discovers the difference, and the language that makes an argument sound as solid as it really is. You will read an original essay in the format of Reading Part 5, listen to an academic on the anatomy of a strong argument in the format of Listening Part 2, and learn nominalisation and word formation, the exact skill tested in Part 3 of the exam. Language focus 2 gives you the impersonal, hedged register of formal writing, and you will plan and write your first proposal. For the Inspiring Nordic project, a well-built argument earns respect that a loud opinion never will. Let's begin.

activities.title: Speaking — Parts 1 and 2. Talk with a partner, then record yourself.

tips.expect: Part 1 (2 minutes): the examiner asks you and your partner questions about yourselves — opinions, studies, free time. Part 2 (about 4 minutes): each of you talks alone for one minute about two of three pictures, answering two questions printed above them; then your partner answers a short question about your pictures (30 seconds).
how: In Part 1, give reasons and an example, not one-word answers — but do not make a speech.
In Part 2, do not just describe the pictures. Compare them and answer both questions: speculate (they might be…, perhaps she's trying to…) and give your view.
Keep talking for the full minute. If you run out of things to say about one picture, move to the second question.

data.text: Part 1: talk about opinions and arguments. Part 2: compare two of the three pictures and say what makes the person's argument convincing.

parts.title: Interview
prompts: When did you last have to argue for an opinion, in speech or in writing? What was it about?
Do you find it easier to argue a point in writing or out loud? Why?
Is there a difference between having an opinion and having an argument? What do you think it is?
Who is the most persuasive person you know? What makes them so convincing?

parts.title: Long turn
parts.question: Compare two of the pictures and say what makes the person's argument convincing and how the situation shapes the language they use.

pictures.caption: a student drafting an essay surrounded by books
a lawyer presenting a case in court
a scientist presenting data at a conference

parts.partner: Which of these arguments do you think would be hardest to prepare? Why? (about 30 seconds)

Comparing: Whereas the lawyer is…, the scientist…
What they have in common is…

activities.title: Vocabulary — argument and academic style. Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.right: turning a verb or adjective into a noun
based on facts rather than personal feelings
existing as an idea, not as a physical thing
exact and clearly defined, with no vagueness
given extra weight because it sounds confident and informed
(of an argument) clear, logical and easy to follow as a whole
to provide evidence that proves or supports a claim
to form the basis or support for a claim or system
showing small but important differences in meaning or judgement
effective at making someone believe or accept something

activities.title: Reading and Use of English Part 5 — multiple choice. Read the essay and choose the answer that fits best.

tips.expect: One long text (about 700–850 words) followed by six four-option questions. They test detail, attitude, purpose, inference and the meaning of ideas in context. The questions follow the order of the text.
how: Read the whole text once, quickly, to get the writer's argument and attitude.
For each question, find the part of the text it refers to and read it closely. The correct option paraphrases the text; wrong options often reuse words from the text but shift the meaning.
Be suspicious of an option that is true in general but is not actually what the writer says.
tips.remember: All four options relate to the right part of the text. Eliminate rather than guessing from the first familiar word.

data.title: Opinions are cheap
data.author: mateo
data.text:
Two weeks ago, in the middle of a class debate about whether social media does more harm than good, I said something I regretted almost as soon as it left my mouth: “It's obviously bad for teenagers.” Nadia, sitting across the room and clearly better prepared than I was, asked a single question: “Obviously how?” I opened my mouth and nothing useful came out. I had an opinion, robustly held and entirely sincere. What I did not have, it turned out, was an argument, and the distance between the two is larger than most of us like to admit. An opinion can be shouted; an argument has to be built, plank by plank, and it has an unpleasant habit of collapsing the moment somebody leans on it. By the end of the lesson, three more people had said much the same sentence in three slightly different ways, and none of us noticed we were doing it.

Miss Vega has a phrase for this that the whole club now uses, sometimes against each other: “That's a conclusion looking for a reason.” An opinion, in her definition, is simply a position — I think X. An argument adds a structure underneath it: a claim, a reason that supports the claim, and evidence that supports the reason. Remove any one of the three and the whole thing tips over. What struck me, rereading my own essays from last year, was how often I had skipped straight from claim to conclusion, treating my own conviction as though it were self-evidently the missing middle step. The essay had a confident voice and almost nothing holding it up, like a bridge painted to look finished before the supports were in place. Sincerity, it turns out, is not evidence. Neither, unfortunately, is repetition.

Evidence is where most arguments quietly die. It is one thing to believe that a policy is unfair; it is quite another to produce a statistic, a documented case or a named authority that a sceptical reader cannot simply wave away. Liam, who treats every claim in class the way a customs officer treats a suitcase, has a habit of asking where a number came from before he accepts what it supposedly proves. Two lessons later, when Sofía quoted a figure about screen time from an article none of us had actually read, Liam simply asked for the source, and the number quietly disappeared from the discussion. Half the time nobody can answer him, myself included. The uncomfortable lesson is that most opinions are held for reasons we have never actually checked — we absorbed them from a parent, a headline or a mood, and mistook the confidence with which we hold them for proof that we are right.

The second thing an argument needs, and an opinion never bothers with, is an opponent. A real argument has to survive contact with the strongest version of the opposing view, not the weakest one. When I finally rewrote my paragraph on social media, I forced myself to state the best case for the other side — that platforms also let isolated teenagers find communities they could never find offline — before explaining why I still thought the costs outweighed the benefits. The paragraph became slower, more qualified, and considerably harder to write. It cost me a whole extra evening, and I am still not sure it was worth the grade, but it changed how I read everything I write now. It also became, for the first time, something a reader might actually be persuaded by, rather than something they could simply agree or disagree with, depending on which side they had already chosen before I opened my mouth.

None of this means that opinions are worthless, or that everyone must footnote every sentence they utter over dinner. It does mean that confidence and correctness are entirely separate qualities, and that the first is a poor substitute for the second, however persuasive it feels from the inside. The people who actually change my mind in a debate are rarely the loudest ones in the room; they are the ones who seem faintly unwilling to be wrong, and check anyway.

For the Inspiring Nordic project, this distinction is not an academic nicety but the whole point of the exercise. An essay that merely announces a position, however elegantly, persuades nobody who did not already agree with it beforehand. Nadia's question has stayed with me for a fortnight now, mostly because I still cannot always answer it. Miss Vega, when I told her this, only smiled and said that doubting your own opinion politely was, in her experience, the beginning of every decent essay she had ever marked. But I have started asking the question of myself before I open my mouth, and my opinions, I like to think, are slightly harder to argue with than they used to be.

An opinion is simply a position. An argument adds a claim, a reason and evidence underneath it. Evidence is where most arguments quietly die: it is one thing to believe a policy is unfair, another to produce a statistic or a named authority. Liam always asks where a number came from before he accepts what it proves. A real argument also needs an opponent: it has to survive contact with the strongest version of the opposing view, not the weakest one. None of this means opinions are worthless, but confidence and correctness are separate qualities. For the Inspiring Nordic project, an essay that merely announces a position persuades nobody who did not already agree with it. Nadia's question has stayed with me, and my opinions are slightly harder to argue with than they used to be.

questions.q: In the first paragraph, the writer describes Nadia's question in order to
options: show that Nadia was trying to embarrass him in front of the class.
introduce the distinction between holding an opinion and having an argument.
explain why classroom debates are usually badly organised.
argue that social media is not actually harmful to teenagers.

questions.q: What does the image of the bridge in the second paragraph suggest about the writer's earlier essays?
options: They were too short to make a convincing case.
They copied ideas from other students' work.
They contained conclusions that were never properly supported.
They avoided giving any clear opinion at all.

questions.q: What does the writer imply about Liam in the third paragraph?
options: He rarely expresses an opinion of his own.
He disagrees with most of what is said in class.
He is unwilling to accept a claim without checking its source.
He finds statistics more persuasive than personal experience.

questions.q: Rewriting the paragraph about social media taught the writer that
options: acknowledging the opposing view can make an argument more persuasive.
it is best to avoid controversial topics in an essay.
readers prefer arguments that reach a firm conclusion quickly.
the strongest arguments avoid mentioning any opposing view.

questions.q: In the fifth paragraph, the writer suggests that the most convincing people in a debate are those who
options: speak with the most confidence and volume.
combine confidence with a willingness to question themselves.
avoid stating a clear opinion until the very end.
rely mainly on emotional appeals to win an argument.

questions.q: What is the writer's main purpose in the final paragraph?
options: to admit that his opinions have not changed at all.
to criticise Nadia for being too demanding in debates.
to explain why the Inspiring Nordic project should be cancelled.
to show how a simple question has changed the way he argues.

activities.title: Language focus 1 — nominalisation and word formation for academic style

data.title: Nominalisation and word formation for academic style
data.can: I can turn verbs and adjectives into abstract nouns to make my writing sound formal, objective and precise, choosing the right ending and negative prefix.
data.intro: Formal and academic English prefers nouns to verbs. By turning actions and qualities into nouns, a writer removes the people from the sentence and sounds objective and compact. Word formation — knowing the noun, verb, adjective and adverb in a family — is the key skill behind this, and the exact skill tested in Part 3 of the exam.

examples.text: The government's failure to act angered voters.
A careful analysis of the data followed.
The clarity of her argument impressed everyone.
The committee reached a decision within the hour.
Her attendance at every meeting was noted.
The growth of the club surprised even Miss Vega.
There has been a sharp rise in applications.
examples.note: compare: prices rose sharply → the sharp rise in prices

rules: Turn a verb or adjective into a noun to sound formal and objective: decide → decision, grow → growth, analyse → analysis.

Common noun endings: -tion/-sion (decide → decision), -ment (improve → improvement), -ance/-ence (assist → assistance, differ → difference), -ity (able → ability), -ness (aware → awareness), -al (arrive → arrival).
Some nouns are irregular, or identical to the verb: rise, fall, increase, change. Learn each family, not just the endings.
A nominalised sentence often needs a different preposition or article from the original verb: prices rose sharply → the sharp rise in prices, not ‘of prices’.
In Part 3, read the whole sentence: the gap may need a noun, verb, adjective, adverb, plural, or a negative form with un-/in-/dis-/im-.
Use nominalisation sparingly: too many abstract nouns in a row make a sentence hard to read. Balance is what real academic writers aim for.

practice.instructions: Choose the correct form of the word in brackets.

items.sentence: The ___ of the bridge took two years. (construct)
We admired the ___ of his prose. (clear)
The ___ of the results was surprising. (analyse)
There has been a steady ___ in numbers this term. (grow)
The judges reached their ___ within the hour. (decide)

activities.title: Reading and Use of English Part 3 — word formation. Use the word in capitals to form a word that fits each gap.

tips.expect: A short text (about 180–230 words) with eight gaps. Each gap has a root word in capitals, which you must change into the correct form — noun, adjective, adverb, negative or plural. One mark per correct answer.
how: Read the whole text first for general meaning before you fill any gap.
Decide what part of speech the gap needs by looking at the words around it — after ‘a/an’ or ‘the’ you usually need a noun; after ‘be’, often an adjective.
Check whether the word needs a negative prefix (un-/in-/dis-/im-) or a plural form: the meaning of the sentence decides, not just the ending that looks natural.
tips.remember: Spelling counts. A correct word spelt wrongly, or the wrong part of speech, earns no mark.

data.title: Building an argument: a checklist
data.text: Miss Vega handed out this short checklist after grading last month's essays, and now asks the whole club to run through it before submitting anything new. First, check that every {1:ARGUE} in your essay is built from a claim, a reason and evidence, not just a strongly held opinion. Second, read your own writing as {2:OBJECT} as you can manage: would a sceptical stranger find your reasoning {3:PERSUADE}, or only your friends? Third, look for {4:EVIDENT} — a statistic, a quotation or a documented case — for every claim that a reader might reasonably doubt. Fourth, note any {5:SIGNIFY} gaps, places where a conclusion appears with no visible support beneath it, and mark each one before you move on. Fifth, be honest about sources that are {6:RELY}, since a single anonymous post is not proof of anything, however often it has been shared. Sixth, check your paragraphs for {7:CONSIST}: does paragraph three quietly contradict what paragraph one claimed? Finally, ask a classmate for their honest {8:ANALYSE} of your conclusion, and listen carefully even when it stings. None of these steps takes more than five minutes, yet together they turn a confident opinion into something closer to a genuine argument.

activities.title: Listening Part 2 — sentence completion. Complete the sentences with a word or short phrase.

tips.expect: A monologue of about three minutes — an interview, a talk or a lecture. You complete eight sentences with a word or short phrase (never more than three words) that you hear. You hear the recording twice.
how: Before it starts, read the eight sentences and predict the kind of word missing: a noun? an adjective? a two-word term?
The sentences follow the order of the recording, and the wording around each gap is paraphrased — but the answer itself is the exact word or words you hear.
Write exactly what you hear, spelt correctly, without changing its form.
tips.remember: If you miss one gap, let it go and follow the next sentence. You have a second listening to fill any gaps.

data.voice_note: Presenter (Ryan) + Dr Priya Anand, linguist, on the language of a strong academic argument.
data.script:
Presenter: You're listening to Page One, and today's guest is Dr Priya Anand, a linguist who has spent the last decade studying how students learn to write academic arguments. Her new book is called Beyond Opinion.
Dr Anand: Thank you for having me. I want to start with something that surprised me when I began this research. Most students I interviewed already knew, in theory, that an essay needs evidence. What they lacked was not knowledge but a habit — the habit of asking themselves a very simple question after every sentence: how do I actually know that.
Dr Anand: In our study, we asked two hundred students to write a short argument and then explain, out loud, why they believed each sentence. The strongest essays, almost without exception, came from students who could answer that question immediately. The weakest essays came from students who paused, and then said something like, I just think it's true.
Dr Anand: The second finding concerns structure. We coded every essay for what we called the reason-evidence gap, the distance between a claim and the proof offered for it. In the top group, that gap was almost always one sentence. In the bottom group, writers often left three or four sentences of pure assertion before any evidence appeared, if it appeared at all.
Dr Anand: What produces a narrow gap? Training helps, but the single strongest factor we measured was something we called audience awareness, how vividly a writer imagined a reader who disagreed with them. Students who pictured a sceptical reader over their shoulder wrote noticeably tighter arguments than students who simply pictured their teacher, who they assumed would be sympathetic anyway.
Dr Anand: There is a myth I would like to correct here. Many students believe that a strong argument requires strong language, words like clearly, obviously, undeniably. Our data shows almost the opposite. Essays full of those intensifiers scored lower on average, because the words were doing the work that evidence should have been doing. The best essays, instead, used what we call hedging, appears to, tends to, is likely to, and readers rated them as more, not less, convincing.
Dr Anand: We also looked at vocabulary. Students who used nominalisation, turning verbs into nouns, like transforming decide into decision, scored higher for formality, but only when they combined it with concrete evidence underneath. Nominalisation without evidence, one of my colleagues likes to say, is just fog with better grammar.
Dr Anand: My final piece of advice for anyone preparing for an exam like C1 Advanced is almost embarrassingly simple. Before you write your conclusion, go back and count your reasons. If you cannot number them on one hand, your argument probably has a gap somewhere, and it is worth finding it before your reader does.
Presenter: Dr Priya Anand, thank you very much.

questions.q: Dr Anand says that most students already understood, in theory, that an essay needs …
She says the weakest students, when asked to justify a sentence, often said that they simply … it was true.
The distance between a claim and its proof is called the reason-evidence …
In the weakest essays, several sentences of pure … came before any evidence.
The strongest single factor measured was something the researchers called …
Many students wrongly believe that a strong argument needs strong …, such as ‘clearly’ or ‘obviously’.
Essays that used hedging language were rated by readers as more …
Nominalisation without evidence is described by a colleague as fog with better …

activities.title: Language focus 2 — impersonal structures and hedging for formal register

data.title: The impersonal, hedged language of formal register
data.can: I can use impersonal structures, hedging and precise formal verbs instead of ‘get’ and phrasal verbs, to make my writing sound formal and academic.
data.intro: Formal, academic English avoids naming ‘I’ or ‘you’ too often, and rarely commits to an absolute claim. Two techniques make this possible: impersonal structures that remove the writer from the sentence, and hedging language that shows caution instead of certainty. Together they are the difference between sounding argumentative and sounding authoritative.

examples.text: It can be argued that nominalisation makes prose sound more objective.
There is a tendency for young writers to overuse abstract nouns.
The results appear to support the original hypothesis.
Such essays tend to rely on personal anecdote rather than evidence.
It would seem that objectivity is harder to achieve than to define.
Rather than ‘the club got better results’, formal style prefers ‘the club's results improved’.
Instead of ‘the report points out a problem’, formal style prefers ‘the report indicates a problem’.

rules: Use impersonal structures to remove yourself from the sentence: There is a tendency for…, It can be argued that…, It is often assumed that…
Hedge instead of asserting absolutely: tend to, appear to, seem to, would suggest, is likely to — softer and more academic than definitely or obviously.
Replace get with a precise formal verb: get better → improve; get bigger → increase, grow; get worse → deteriorate.
Prefer a single formal verb to a phrasal verb: find out → discover; point out → indicate; bring about → cause; put off → postpone.
Avoid contractions and direct address (you, your) in formal writing; use one, readers, or an impersonal structure instead.
Combine hedging with nominalisation for maximum effect: There is a tendency towards a rise in prices sounds even more academic than prices tend to rise.

practice.instructions: Choose the more formal option to complete each sentence.

items.sentence: It ___ that nominalisation is a hallmark of academic prose.
Researchers ___ that the sample size had affected the results.
There is a ___ for students to avoid the passive voice unnecessarily.
The new measures ___ to have solved the problem.
The report will ___ several serious weaknesses in the plan.

activities.title: Reading and Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations

tips.expect: Six sentences. For each one you complete a second sentence with the same meaning as the first, using a given key word that must not change. You write between three and six words, including the key word. Each item is worth up to two marks.
how: Identify what is being tested — here, mostly nominalisation, but also collocations and fixed phrases.
Write the whole gap, then read the complete second sentence: does it mean exactly the same as the first? Is the key word unchanged?
Count your words. Contractions count as two words (doesn't = does not).
tips.remember: Half marks exist: if the structure is right but a small word is wrong, you can still score one mark.

data.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first sentence, using the word given. Do not change the word given. You must use between three and six words, including the word given.

items.first: Mateo argued his point clearly, and the whole club was convinced.
Researchers discovered new evidence, and this strengthened the theory.
It is often said that students avoid nominalisation because it sounds unnatural.
Nadia analysed the results carefully before she reached a conclusion.
The reading club grew quickly, which pleased Miss Vega.
Many people believe that the government failed to prepare properly, and this caused the crisis.

activities.title: Writing Part 2 — proposal. Plan, write 220–260 words and hand it in.

tips.expect: Part 2 offers a choice of formats — article, email/letter, report, review or proposal. A proposal recommends action to a specific reader (a teacher, a manager, a committee) and normally uses section headings. 220–260 words, formal or semi-formal register.
how: Use clear section headings (Introduction, Current situation, Suggestions, Recommendation) instead of essay-style paragraphs with no titles.
Support each suggestion with a reason, not just a list of ideas — a proposal has to persuade, not just inform.
Use the impersonal and hedged language of Language focus 2 (there is a tendency to…, it could be argued that…) instead of a string of ‘I think’s.
End with one clear recommendation. A proposal that lists options but never decides loses marks for communicative achievement.
tips.remember: The examiner marks content, communicative achievement, organisation and language. A proposal without headings, or without a final recommendation, does not fully achieve the task, however good the English.

data.task:
Your English teacher, Miss Vega, has asked the C1 reading club to suggest ways of making written feedback on each other's essays more useful. She will read the best proposals aloud in class.

Some ideas raised in the club meeting:

  • a fixed feedback form with sentence starters
  • swapping essays between different reading pairs each time
  • a short face-to-face conversation after written comments

Write a proposal for Miss Vega. Describe the current problem, evaluate two of the ideas above (or your own), and end with a clear recommendation. Write 220–260 words.
plan: Introduction (1–2 sentences): state the purpose of the proposal — why you are writing and what problem it addresses. No suggestions yet.
Current situation: describe the problem in more detail, using one specific example from your own experience of the club.
Suggestions: evaluate two ideas (from the notes or your own). For each, give one advantage and one possible drawback, using hedging language.
Recommendation: choose the strongest idea, or a combination, and say clearly why, using nominalisation and confident but formal language.

Introducing the proposal: The purpose of this proposal is to…
Following our discussion, I would like to suggest…
Describing the problem: At present, there is a tendency for…
Evaluating an idea: One advantage of this approach is that…
A possible drawback, however, is that…
This would appear to solve the problem, although…
Recommending: It is this option that seems most likely to…
For these reasons, I would strongly suggest…

checklist: I have used clear headings instead of untitled paragraphs.
I have described the problem before suggesting any solution.
I have evaluated exactly two ideas, each with an advantage and a drawback.
My recommendation is clear and comes at the end.
I have used at least one impersonal structure and one nominalisation from this unit.
Between 220 and 260 words, in a formal register with no contractions.
data.model:
A model answer (245 words). Notice the four clear sections and the single final recommendation.

Introduction

The purpose of this proposal is to suggest how the reading club could make written feedback on essays more useful, following our discussion at the last meeting.

Current situation

At present, feedback tends to consist of a single word in the margin, good or vague, which tells a writer very little about how to improve. Last term, for instance, three separate essays repeated the same overused link words, and none of the writers found out until Miss Vega mentioned it in front of the whole class. There is also a tendency for written comments to be misread as harsher than intended, since tone is difficult to judge on paper alone.

Suggestions

Two ideas were raised. The first, a fixed feedback form with sentence starters such as, your strongest paragraph is, would ensure that every comment is specific and constructive; a possible drawback is that it might feel mechanical if it were used too rigidly. The second, a short face-to-face conversation after written comments, allows misunderstandings to be clarified immediately, although it would require more time than a written note alone.

Recommendation

On balance, I would recommend combining the two: a short form for structure, followed by two minutes of conversation whenever possible. This combination addresses both the vagueness and the tone of current feedback while remaining realistic about the time available, and it is this balance, rather than either idea alone, that seems most likely to raise the standard of our essays this year.

activities.title: Speaking — Parts 3 and 4. Collaborative task and discussion. Record your best answer.

tips.expect: Part 3 (about 4 minutes): you and your partner discuss a question with five written prompts for two minutes, then have one minute to reach a decision. Part 4 (about 5 minutes): the examiner asks you both wider questions on the same theme.
how: In Part 3 you are not marked on agreeing; you are marked on interacting — ask your partner's opinion, respond to it, build on it, disagree politely.
Do not try to cover all five prompts. Two or three in real depth beats five in a rush.
In the decision minute, negotiate: Shall we agree that…? I'd go along with that, as long as…
In Part 4, develop your answers: opinion → reason → example → so what.
tips.remember: Look at your partner, not at the examiner. The examiner is listening, not talking.

data.text: Part 3: discuss how these things might strengthen an argument and decide which is easiest to misuse or exaggerate. Part 4: discuss persuasion, objectivity and knowing what to believe.

parts.title: Collaborative task
parts.intro: Here are some things that can be used to strengthen an argument. Talk to each other about how each of these might make an argument more convincing.
parts.centre: How might these strengthen an argument?
parts.decide: Now you have a minute to decide which of these is easiest to misuse or exaggerate.

parts.title: Further discussion
prompts: Some people say that with enough confidence, you can argue almost anything convincingly. Do you agree?
Should schools teach students how to construct an argument as a subject in itself?
Is it becoming harder or easier to tell a well-supported argument from a merely confident one, in the age of social media?
Do you think complete objectivity is actually possible, or does everyone argue from some hidden point of view?
How can someone tell the difference between a strong argument and simple stubbornness?

Involving your partner: Would you go along with that?
That's true up to a point, although…
Building on an idea: Following on from what you said…
Reaching a decision: I'd be inclined to go for…, on the grounds that…
We could agree to differ, but if we had to choose…
Part 4: developing an answer: There's a strong case for saying…
Rarely is it as simple as…

homework.prompt: Write a short academic paragraph (10–12 sentences) turning one of your own opinions into a structured argument for the Inspiring Nordic project. Use at least four nominalisations (e.g. decision, growth, analysis, failure) and at least one impersonal or hedging structure from Language focus 2 (there is a tendency to…, it could be argued that…). Capital letters and full stops!
